name: Pharmacogenomics
title: Pharmacogenomics
answer: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how inherited and acquired genetic variation changes a person's response to medicines, from the speed at which a drug is metabolized to the risk of an adverse reaction. It sits inside genomic medicine and precision therapeutics, and it draws on clinical pharmacology, laboratory medicine, and informatics. The work covers single-gene tests, such as those for CYP2D6 or TPMT, as well as multigene panels that a clinician might order before starting a treatment. In this atlas it belongs with the AI physician because many of the models tracked here are built to predict a phenotype from a genotype or to flag a drug-gene interaction at the point of care.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Pharmacogenomics is the study of how inherited and acquired genetic variation changes a person's response to medicines, from the speed at which a drug is metabolized to the risk of an adverse reaction. It sits inside genomic medicine and precision therapeutics, and it draws on clinical pharmacology, laboratory medicine, and informatics. The work covers single-gene tests, such as those for CYP2D6 or TPMT, as well as multigene panels that a clinician might order before starting a treatment. In this atlas it belongs with the AI physician because many of the models tracked here are built to predict a phenotype from a genotype or to flag a drug-gene interaction at the point of care.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The physical and computational base includes genotyping arrays, short-read and long-read sequencers, and the laboratory information systems that move a sample from accessioning to a signed report. Reference resources such as PharmGKB and the CPIC guidelines are consulted at the bench and embedded in clinical decision support. On the AI side, the site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 797 scientific models, and a small share of those are trained on pharmacogenomic variant data or on electronic health records linked to medication outcomes. Compute for training and inference typically runs on GPU clusters, either on premises or in a cloud environment, with the resulting models served through an API or a rules engine inside the electronic health record.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a specimen, usually blood or saliva, and a decision about which genes or variants to interrogate. Laboratory staff extract DNA, run the assay, and call variants against a reference genome, then a clinical scientist or genetic counselor assigns a diplotype and translates it into a predicted phenotype, such as poor, intermediate, normal, or rapid metabolizer. AI enters at several points: machine learning models can prioritize variants of uncertain significance, natural language processing can mine the literature for new drug-gene pairs, and graph models can represent interactions among genes, drugs, and pathways. The final step is a clinical decision support message that a prescriber sees alongside the order, but the interpretation and the prescribing decision remain with the clinician.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in pharmacogenomics turn on consent, data privacy, and the provenance of the reference data used to make a call. A laboratory report may be governed by CLIA and CAP accreditation in the United States, and by GDPR or other privacy regimes elsewhere, while the patient's genetic data carries implications for relatives who never consented to testing. The site tracks 218 compliance and regulation pages and 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows that the legal exposure around algorithmic decision support is real and still being defined. Provenance matters because a model trained on one ancestral population may perform poorly on another, and because guideline versions change, so a report must state which evidence base it used.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving from reactive, single-gene tests toward preemptive genotyping, where a panel is ordered once and stored for later prescribing decisions. AI is likely to be used to scale interpretation, to combine pharmacogenomic variants with polygenic scores and clinical variables, and to monitor real-world outcomes after a drug is prescribed. Regulators and professional societies are working on how to validate and update these models, and the lawsuits mentioned above may shape what evidence a developer must show. For a working professional, the practical shift is that pharmacogenomic results will appear more often inside the electronic health record, not as a separate consult, and the challenge will be keeping the underlying knowledge current.
